title: Spillages: blood, body fluids & mercury
blurb: How to deal safely with blood and body fluid spills using the spill kit, and why a mercury spill needs a completely different approach.
question: In one morning, a patient's blood drips onto the surgery floor after an extraction, and later an amalgam capsule pops open after mixing, scattering tiny silver beads across the worktop. How do you deal with each spill, and what must you never do?

teach.h: Two kinds of spill, two different dangers
teach.body: Spills in a dental practice fall into two groups. Blood and body fluids (saliva, vomit, urine) are an infection risk because they can carry blood-borne viruses and other micro-organisms. Mercury from amalgam is a chemical risk: it gives off a toxic vapour that you breathe in. Each has its own spill kit and procedure, assessed under COSHH. Know where the kits are, what's in them, and follow the instructions inside every time.

rows.label: Never
values: Use a mop from another area

steps.label: Make the area safe
steps.sub: Keep people away from the spill

steps.label: Put on PPE
steps.sub: Apron, eye protection if splashes are likely, then gloves

steps.label: Cover and absorb
steps.sub: Use the kit's granules or absorbent; leave for the stated time

steps.label: Scoop it up
steps.sub: Scraper and scoop into a clinical waste bag

steps.label: Clean, then disinfect
steps.sub: Detergent and water, then disinfect as your policy sets

steps.label: Dispose, PPE off, hand hygiene
steps.sub: Infectious waste; restock the kit; record it

teach.h: Follow the kit, not a guess
teach.body: Many spill kits use chlorine-releasing granules or solutions. They only work at the right strength and with the right contact time, so the concentration and timing come from your practice policy and the spill kit instructions, never from guesswork. They are hazardous chemicals too: don't mix them with other products, and don't use them on urine, because harmful chlorine gas can be released. Ventilate the area, and check the COSHH assessment for the product you're using.

items.label: Biohazard
items.sub: Blood and body fluids, clinical waste

teach.caption: Check the safety data sheet and COSHH assessment before using any spill-kit chemical.

steps.label: Keep people away and ventilate
steps.sub: Open windows; turn off any heating nearby

steps.label: Collect it with the mercury kit
steps.sub: Absorbent paste or sponge; never vacuum or sweep

steps.label: Dispose as hazardous waste
steps.sub: Following the practice amalgam waste policy

steps.label: Report and record
steps.sub: Large spill: follow policy for specialist help

teach.body: Liquid mercury breaks into tiny beads that roll into cracks and keep releasing vapour, and warmth makes this worse. A vacuum cleaner heats the mercury and blows vapour round the room, and a brush scatters the beads further. Prevention helps most: use pre-encapsulated amalgam, check capsules before and after mixing, mix only in a closed amalgamator, and keep clinical floors sealed with no carpet. Amalgam waste goes in a white container with mercury suppressant.

rows.label: Pick up mercury beads with bare fingers
Use chlorine granules on a urine spill
Open windows after a mercury spill
Leave granules for the kit's stated contact time

teach.text: Never vacuum or sweep mercury. Never guess the strength of a disinfectant or put chlorine products on urine. The spill kit instructions and practice policy decide what you use and for how long.

items: Blood spills are an infection risk; mercury spills are a toxic vapour risk.
Blood: area safe, PPE, cover and absorb, scoop, clean then disinfect, infectious waste.
Strength and contact time come from the spill kit and practice policy.
Mercury: ventilate, PPE, mercury spill kit, seal, hazardous waste, report.
Never vacuum or brush mercury, and never use chlorine products on urine.

summary: You can now tell the infection risk of a blood spill from the chemical risk of a mercury spill, work through each spill procedure in the right order with the right PPE, and avoid the dangerous mistakes: vacuuming mercury, guessing disinfectant strength and putting chlorine on urine.

A.q: A small amount of blood is spilled on the surgery floor. What is the correct approach?
options: Mop it up with the kitchen mop
Follow the blood spillage procedure
Cover it with paper towels and leave it to dry
Wipe it with a dry paper towel
A.why: Every blood spill, however small, is dealt with using the blood spillage procedure, spill kit and appropriate PPE.

whyNot.0: A kitchen mop would spread contamination between areas.
whyNot.2: Leaving it covered doesn't make it safe or clean.
whyNot.3: A dry towel doesn't disinfect the area and isn't the procedure.

A.q: During amalgam placement, the capsule opens unexpectedly after mixing and mercury spills on the worktop. What is the best action?
options: Sweep it into the sink
Vacuum it up straight away
Pick up the beads with your bare fingers
Contain it with the mercury spill kit
A.why: Follow the mercury spill policy: ventilate, wear PPE and use the mercury spill kit to contain and collect it.

whyNot.0: Mercury must never go down the sink; it's hazardous waste.
whyNot.1: Vacuuming heats and spreads mercury vapour.
whyNot.2: Mercury should never be handled with bare skin.

A.q: Why must a vacuum cleaner never be used on a mercury spill?
options: It would block the filter
Mercury damages the motor
It spreads mercury vapour
Mercury is too heavy to lift
A.why: A vacuum warms the mercury and blows vapour into the air, increasing the amount breathed in.

whyNot.0: The concern is vapour exposure, not a blocked filter.
whyNot.1: Damage to the machine is not the main reason.
whyNot.3: A vacuum can lift mercury; the problem is the vapour it spreads.

B.q: Which PPE should be worn to deal with a blood spill on the floor?
options: Gloves, apron and eye protection if needed
Gloves only, because it is just a small spill
No PPE if you use the scoop
A mask only, to avoid the smell
B.why: Gloves and an apron protect hands and clothing; eye protection is added if splashing is likely.

whyNot.1: Spills of any size need an apron as well as gloves.
whyNot.2: Using a scoop doesn't remove the need for PPE.
whyNot.3: A mask alone leaves hands and clothing unprotected.

B.q: Why should chlorine-releasing granules not be used on a spill of urine?
options: They stain the floor yellow
Urine cancels out their disinfecting action
Harmful chlorine gas may be released
They take too long to work
B.why: Chlorine-releasing products can react with urine and give off harmful chlorine gas.

whyNot.0: Staining isn't the reason; the gas is.
whyNot.1: The danger is a chemical reaction producing gas.
whyNot.3: Speed isn't the issue; safety is.

B.q: After absorbing and scooping up a blood spill, where should the waste go?
options: Domestic black bag, double-bagged
Recycling bin
Sharps container
Infectious clinical waste
B.why: Blood-contaminated spill waste is infectious clinical waste and goes in the correct clinical waste bag.

whyNot.0: Black bags are for domestic waste only.
whyNot.2: Sharps containers are for sharps, not absorbent and paper towels.

C.q: How do you know which disinfectant strength and contact time to use on a blood spill?
options: Judge it by how big the spill looks
Ask the patient involved
Use the strongest possible mix
Follow the kit and practice policy
C.why: The spill kit instructions and practice policy set the product, strength and contact time.

whyNot.0: Guessing risks too weak a mix or a dangerous one.
whyNot.1: Patients don't decide infection control procedures.
whyNot.2: Stronger isn't better: it can damage surfaces and harm staff.

C.q: What should be done in the room straight after a mercury spill?
options: Ventilate it and keep others away
Turn the heating up to dry it
Close the windows to contain the vapour
Carry on treating the patient
C.why: Ventilation reduces vapour levels, and keeping people away limits exposure while the spill is cleared.

whyNot.2: Closing windows keeps vapour in the room with you.
whyNot.3: The spill must be made safe first.

C.q: Which hazard pictogram warns that a substance, such as mercury, can be fatal if inhaled?
options: Biohazard
Skull and crossbones
Flame
Corrosion
C.why: The skull and crossbones shows acute toxicity, such as 'fatal if inhaled' for mercury.

whyNot.0: The biohazard sign marks infectious material such as blood.
whyNot.3: The corrosion symbol marks substances that burn skin or metal.

reteach.title: Germs or poison?
reteach.question: Before you reach for a spill kit, ask one question: is this a germ problem or a poison problem? How does that tell you what to do?

blocks.body: Blood, saliva and vomit are a germ problem: you need a barrier (PPE), something to absorb and disinfect, and infectious waste disposal. Mercury is a poison problem: the danger is in the air, so you ventilate, avoid anything that heats or scatters it, and seal it away as hazardous waste. Once you've named the danger, the right kit and the right steps follow.

blocks.text: The spill kit's instructions are the rule book: strength, contact time and disposal all come from them and your practice policy.

explain.body: Make the area safe, put on PPE, cover and absorb with the spill kit, scoop up, clean with detergent then disinfect as policy sets, and dispose of everything as infectious waste.

test.q: What is the first thing to do when you find a blood spill on the floor?
options: Pour bleach straight onto it
Mop it with hot soapy water
Keep people away; put on PPE
Cover it with a clean bib
test.why: First make the area safe and protect yourself, then use the spill kit as instructed.

whyNot.0: Neat bleach is not the procedure and can be dangerous.
whyNot.1: Mopping spreads blood and isn't the spill procedure.
whyNot.3: Covering with a bib doesn't absorb or disinfect it safely.

explain.body: Chlorine-releasing products work only at the right strength and contact time, set by the kit and practice policy. Never mix them with other products or use them on urine.

test.q: Which statement about chlorine-releasing disinfectants is correct?
options: They are safe to mix with any cleaner
Use the strength and time the kit states
They work instantly with no contact time
They are the best choice for urine
test.why: These products must be used at the strength and contact time set by the kit instructions and practice policy.

whyNot.2: They need the stated contact time to work.
whyNot.3: They can release chlorine gas with urine.

explain.body: Ventilate and keep people away, wear PPE, collect the mercury with the mercury spill kit, seal it in a labelled container, dispose of it as hazardous waste, and report it. Never vacuum, sweep or touch it.

test.q: Which should you use to collect mercury droplets after a spill?
options: The mercury spill kit
A vacuum cleaner
A dustpan and brush
A wet kitchen mop
test.why: The mercury spill kit contains materials to collect and contain mercury safely without spreading vapour.

whyNot.1: Vacuuming heats and spreads mercury vapour.
whyNot.3: A mop spreads mercury and contaminates the mop.
